title: The last four petitions (CCC 2828–2854)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first three petitions: thy name, thy kingdom, thy will. Your line was thy, thy, thy. Did you manage to speak about someone else first? Day one thousand one hundred fifty.

The Douay-Rheims Bible gives the same loaf of bread two different names. In Luke's Gospel, the Our Father asks, "Give us this day our daily bread." Turn back to Matthew, same prayer, and the Douay-Rheims reads, "Give us this day our supersubstantial bread." Supersubstantial. A word nobody uses at the bakery. It isn't a typo, and it isn't careless. It sits right on top of a real puzzle in the prayer, and the Catechism walks straight into it. The prayer has just turned toward God three times. Now it turns toward us. Today: the last four petitions.
screen: `DAILY BREAD, IN LUKE.` → `SUPERSUBSTANTIAL, IN MATTHEW.` → `NOW THE PRAYER TURNS TO US.`

segments.voice: Give. The Catechism notes that the Greek word behind daily, epiousios, appears nowhere else in the New Testament. Read one way, it points to time: bread for this day, enough for now. Read more literally, it points beyond ordinary bread, to the bread of life, which Catholics understand as Christ himself in the Eucharist. The Church keeps both. Bread for the table, and bread for the soul. Forgive. "And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors." The Catechism calls this petition astonishing, and it leans on the small word as. God's mercy, it says, can't get into a heart that refuses to forgive. Not because God's mercy is small, but because a closed heart is closed. Lead. "And lead us not into temptation." The line raises a question. Does God lead anyone into temptation? The letter of James answers flatly: "God is not a tempter of evils, and he tempteth no man." The Catechism says the Greek carries two shades: don't let us enter into temptation, and don't let us give in to it. Deliver. "But deliver us from evil." Here the Catechism says evil isn't only an idea. It names a person, the evil one, who opposes God. And it reads the petition as asking to be freed from all evil, past, present and future, of which he is the author. Give, forgive, lead, deliver. Four requests, all plural. Us, not me.
screen: `GIVE: BREAD FOR TODAY, AND MORE.` · `FORGIVE: AS WE FORGIVE.` · `LEAD: GOD TEMPTS NO ONE.` · `DELIVER: FROM THE EVIL ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for your daily bread. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself what you actually need for today. Not this year, not this month. Today. Maybe it's food. Maybe it's patience, or one honest conversation, or rest. Name it simply. Then think of one other person who needs bread today, of any kind. If you pray, you can say, "Give us this day our daily bread," with both of you in the us. If you don't, hold them side by side. The bell holds the time.
The last four petitions. In the Our Father: give us bread, forgive us as we forgive, lead us not into temptation, deliver us from evil. Today's words.
Your line: give, forgive, lead, deliver. Today, notice how often you say I and me when you ask for things, and try saying us once. Day one thousand one hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Catholics pray these petitions in every Our Father; at Mass it is said just before Communion, and some hear 'our daily bread' there as pointing to the Eucharist as well as ordinary food.

what a scholar hears: epiousios appears nowhere else in the New Testament, the Catechism notes; the Church reads it both as daily and, literally, as the bread of life.

notes: CCC 2828–2854 paraphrased (copyrighted English). Check: epiousios occurring nowhere else in the New Testament, its temporal and literal ('super-essential') senses, the bread of life (2837); 'as' being astonishing and mercy unable to penetrate an unforgiving heart (2838, 2840); the Greek meaning both 'do not allow us to enter' and 'do not let us yield to' temptation, and James 1:13 (2846); evil as a person, Satan, the Evil One, and deliverance from all evils, past, present and future, of which he is the author (2851, 2854).
Douay-Rheims: confirm Luke 11:3 reads 'daily bread' and Matthew 6:11 'supersubstantial bread' in the Challoner text; confirm Matthew 6:12–13 and James 1:13 wording.
'Four requests, all plural' refers to the 'us' and 'our' in each line; confirm.
howItsDone: the Our Father at Mass falls in the Communion rite; confirm phrasing.
